rv.q: the new production deftly underscores the parallels of our current ugly political divide
Whatever the limit of the Gold shenanigans, they all feel very much in service of the message of a prescient play about the dangers of populist manipulation by those invested in the status quo.
Clearly, MTC has lucked out with its timing of this classic drama, its Victorian-era polemics ordinarily a bit simplistic — but given the peculiar insanity of election politics, right on the money.
Nor does it make sense that they would object to Sam Gold’s crackling and persuasive production, which drove those views home despite having to regroup once the protesters were ejected.

But she, director Doug Hughes and this first-rate cast -- headed by Boyd Gaines and Richard Thomas -- are true to both the playwright and to theatergoers hungry for a play as wise about human nature as it is entertaining.
The production succeeds in making Ibsen's 1882 drama feel immediate and urgent, though it can't quite overcome the play's inherent didacticism.
Boyd Gaines delivers a passionate, beautifully modulated performance as Dr. Stockmann, the idealistic physician who discovers that his town's profitable spa waters are contaminated.

But in this production, it isn't clear why anyone should want to join him in the first place.

Theatre Club production also has a huge asset in leading man Boyd Gaines, whose Thomas is a distinctly earthbound but still mesmerizing force of nature -- by turns formidable, frail, frazzled, funny and tragic.
